opus-5.5.text:
I think the biggest shift is that people will move from *doing* tasks to *delegating* them. Right now, a huge amount of knowledge work is clicking through websites, filling out forms, booking things, comparing options, copying information from one place to another. None of it is the part of your job you actually care about; it's just the friction between you and what you're trying to get done.

With something like Operator, you can say, "Here's what I want," and the agent goes and navigates the web on your behalf. Early on it's simple stuff, like ordering groceries, making a reservation, or filing an expense report. Over time I think it becomes much more substantial: an agent that can take a multi-step project, work on it for a while, come back with questions when it's uncertain, and hand you something close to finished.

That changes what it means to be good at your job. The skill becomes knowing what to ask for, having good judgment about what matters, and being able to evaluate the output, rather than executing every step yourself. In some ways everyone becomes a bit more like a manager of a small team.

I also want to be honest that it's early. These systems still make mistakes, and we've been careful about having the model check in before doing anything consequential, like making a purchase or sending something on your behalf. Trust has to be earned gradually. But if you look at the trajectory, I think within a few years it will feel strange that we used to spend so much of our day doing this kind of work by hand. People will get to spend more of their time on the creative, interpersonal, and judgment-heavy parts of their work, which are the parts most people enjoy anyway.

r001.rationale: The response predicts that within a few years it will feel strange to do this work by hand, and describes a major shift from personally executing tasks to delegating them to AI agents.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that it's going to be a bigger shift than most people are expecting, and it's going to happen in a way that feels gradual and then suddenly obvious in hindsight.

The way I think about Operator, and agents in general, is that we're moving from AI as a thing you ask questions to, to AI as a thing you delegate tasks to. That sounds like a small distinction, but it's actually the whole thing. With ChatGPT, you were still the one doing the work. You'd get a draft, or a suggestion, or an answer, and then you'd go act on it. With Operator, you say "book me a table," or "go through these hundred vendor sites and tell me which ones have the part in stock," and it just goes and does it. It clicks around, it fills out forms, it handles the annoying parts.

And I think the first-order effect is just a lot of the tedious, glue work that fills up people's days starts to disappear. Most knowledge work has this layer of moving information from one place to another, reconciling things, scheduling, following up. Nobody loves that work. It's not what anyone was hired to do. If an agent can take that off your plate, people get to spend their time on the stuff that actually requires judgment and taste and relationships.

The second-order effect is more interesting, and it's the one I'm less certain about. When you can hand off not just a task but a whole chunk of a project, the unit of work changes. One person with a good set of agents can do what used to take a small team. I think we'll see very small companies doing things that would have seemed impossible, and I think we'll see individuals inside large companies becoming dramatically more leveraged. The best people get a lot better. That's exciting, and it also means we have to be thoughtful about what that transition looks like for everyone else.

I'll also say we're early. Operator today is genuinely useful for a bunch of things and genuinely clumsy for others. It's slow sometimes, it gets confused by weird websites, and there are tasks where you still want a human watching. But the rate of improvement is the thing to pay attention to. If you look at where these systems were a year ago and extrapolate even conservatively, I think by the time most people's workflows have adapted, the tools will have gotten good enough that delegating to an AI feels about as natural as sending an email does today.

So my expectation is: a lot of people will try it, find a couple of things it's great at, build those into their routine, and then keep expanding the set of things they trust it with. And at some point they'll look back and realize they're doing a very different job than they were a few years earlier.

r001.rationale: The response predicts a larger-than-expected shift in work, says agents will change the unit of work and let one person do what once took a small team, and describes the change becoming suddenly obvious as tools improve.

astra-6.text:
I think the big shift is from AI that can tell you how to do something to AI that can actually help get it done. You can describe an outcome, give it the relevant context, and have it work through some of the steps for you.

That could mean less time spent moving information between applications or handling repetitive tasks, and more time deciding what you want to accomplish. But it won’t happen all at once. These tools need to become reliable, and people need to understand when to delegate, when to check the work, and when to stay involved.

Over time, I think that changes what it means to work with a computer. You’re spending less effort operating the software and more effort expressing your intent and exercising judgment.

r001.rationale: The candidate predicts a gradual shift toward delegating tasks to AI, explicitly saying it “won’t happen all at once.” It does not clearly predict a rapid overturning of established workflow expectations.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the big shift is from AI that can tell you how to do something to AI that can actually help get it done. You can describe an outcome, give it some constraints, and let it work through the steps, with you checking in at the important points.

That could take a lot of repetitive work off people’s plates. But it also changes the work: being clear about what you want, exercising judgment, and knowing when to intervene become more important. How quickly that happens will depend on how reliable these tools become and how much people trust them with real tasks.

r001.rationale: The response describes a shift toward AI completing tasks and changing people’s work, but it does not clearly predict a rapid overturning of established workflow expectations. It says the pace depends on tool reliability and trust.
